newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Doyle back in "dear, dirty old Dublin".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Doyle back in "dear, dirty old Dublin".

text.p: Award-winning Irish writer Roddy Doyle, whose first book "The Commitments" became a hit film, has climbed into the head of a 96-year-old man and is not sure if he will make it out again.

For this critically acclaimed and commercially successful writer has utterly immersed himself in his latest hero, an old man who lives through all the 20th century tumults that gave birth to the modern Ireland.

After reading from his latest work in progress at the Frankfurt book fair, he confessed: "I've written 25,000 words and may never be finished. I will finish it somewhere in the next millennium or I might have to throw it in the bin and start something else."

But this quiet and unpretentious writer brought the house down with a riotous account from "The Last Roundup" of how his hero's father, a one-legged Dublin drunk, first met his mother when she accidentally knocked him over in the street.
In his mind, Doyle never strays far from the streets of "dear, dirty old Dublin" and that is the secret of his success.

He was the first to admit that at the world's biggest book fair which this year took Ireland and its Diaspora -- the 78 million Irish exiles around the world from New York to Sydney -- as its main theme.

"Dublin is where I want to live and that is where I am staying. People leave you alone. People don't bother you. I'm about as famous as I'll ever be there unless I kill someone," said the 38-year-old novelist.
Doyle, for 14 years a teacher in North Dublin, made his reputation with a bawdy trilogy about the working class area he knew so well.
He hawked "The Commitments" around publishers who never even opened it. In the end he published it himself and met his future wife when she helped to publicise it.
The riotous tale of how a Dublin group tried to bring James Brown soul music to the slums was turned into a film hit by English director Alan Parker.
The next two books in the trilogy -- "The Snapper" and "The Van" -- were also made into successful films.

In the trilogy, Doyle revelled in the power of dialogue. The hugely entertaining and funny books could easily be read at one sitting. Critics said that if you took out the expletives, they would be no longer than pamphlets.
But then he changed his style with "Paddy Clarke Ha Ha Ha" in which he regressed into the mind of a 10-year-old boy whose parents' marriage was crumbling before his confused young eyes.
The book was an instant bestseller and won Doyle the Booker Prize, Britain's most famous literary award.
His tip to future would-be winners: "Borrow a dinner suit and your father's cufflinks. I did. After that I bought a dinner suit and haven't won anything since."
Next came "The Woman who walked into doors," the bleak tale of a woman whose marriage dissolves when her husband starts to beat her up.

"It took me a long time afterwards to get her voice out of my head. For a while I thought I would have to write 'Woman who walked into doors II' or maybe do an annual pamphlet like a Stephen King serialisation."
Doyle has absolutely no regrets about giving up his job as a geography teacher. "The River Shannon flows in the same direction every year. It got boring. I don't miss it all."

He has written the screenplays for his novels and penned a controversial television serial about a Dublin Family. But first and foremost he sees himself as a novelist revelling in his financial independence.
"I can pick and choose and work at my own pace. I am a novelist who does the odd bit of screenwriting. Essentially I am a writer. It is far more captivating and energising."
There is no need to suffer for your art, gaze endlessly into your soul and either emigrate from Ireland or stay behind and get uproariously drunk.

"One of the old myths was that you had to emigrate (like Oscar Wilde and James Joyce). The other was that you were loud and drunk (like Brendan Behan) and then put pen to paper. I have no times for these myths at all."
